Either decision keeps Lilt alive for now; neither makes the borrowed power disappear. Somewhere far from this quiet moon, a greenhouse is cooling while your bridge is warm.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Lilt consented to a reversible transfer into a portable field lattice. Return to Mara at Hearth to trace its borrowed power.

journal.title: The size of a passenger
journal.text: Spend 60 credits on a portable field lattice. Let Lilt set the stop signal.

journal.title: Arrived at Hearth Station
journal.text: The crossing took 2 days and 2 fuel.

journal.title: Someone else’s winter
journal.text:
Mara lays two maintenance charts side by side. Cinder's emergency supply comes from Low Tide, a tidal farm that signed an agreement to support an empty shield until its final shutdown. The signature is real. So is the phrase EMPTY INSTALLATION. The form never imagined an installation might become occupied without anyone arriving.

"Nobody had to steal the power," she says. "They simply kept honoring an agreement after its meaning changed." Low Tide's operators have already reduced their night heating. No one told them why. Their automatic reports describe this as voluntary conservation, because the contract allows conservation before it allows a missed delivery.

You can send a preliminary finding immediately or wait for a more complete diagnosis. Mara recommends an honest incomplete report: a new possible person, an identifiable cost, no magical answer. "The minute we call this solved, somebody stops looking for the part we haven't solved."

Sera has offered to convene the local partners at Interval Anchorage. She has not ordered a shutdown. A short private message follows the invitation: I asked whether there was someone. You answered. Now help me answer everyone else. Mara studies that sentence before forwarding it to your log. "Good. She put the difficult question in writing too."

journal.title: Someone else’s winter
journal.text: Publish the provisional findings, including Low Tide’s unconsented burden.

journal.title: The other side of an answer
journal.text:
When the bridge clears, Mara asks to hear Lilt's original request once more. Not its technical details. The sentence about being noticed. She listens with the concentration she gives a faint vibration inside a hull.

"I had a brother at a relief station," she says. "Three registers listed him as evacuated. He was. From the reactor room to a pressure shelter. From the shelter to a loading bay. From the loading bay to a transport that had already gone. All the entries were correct about a direction. None was correct about where he was."

She has no recording of his final words. She dislikes people who assume this makes every mysterious voice a second chance. "If Lilt starts sounding like him, I need you to remind me that familiarity isn't identity. I want to help whoever is here. I don't want to turn them into somebody I lost."

The extra chair remains empty. Mara rests a hand on its back and gives you a tired smile. "Don't make this a solemn ritual. I stole it from stores because the quartermaster said we were at capacity. If our mission succeeds, I intend to steal several more." She opens the partner directory. Every contact on it represents another claim on the same finite warmth.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Mara warned against mistaking familiar memories for a returned person. Attend the partner meeting at Interval.

journal.title: The other side of an answer
journal.text: "We help the person who answers. We do not tell them who to be."

journal.title: Arrived at Interval Anchorage
journal.text: The crossing took 2 days and 3 fuel.

journal.title: The unfinished envoy
journal.text:
The Chmmr envoy greets you in two tones separated by a fraction of a second. "I am Ilex," says the first. "And the space in which Ilex is not finished speaking," says the second. The combined translation settles on ILEX / INTERVAL. "This is not a medical emergency," they add before your scanner can be tactful about it.

Their synthesis was accelerated in the war that freed Earth. They do not regret that freedom. They do not regard its costs as an argument for slavery. They simply live with an unfinished negotiation between inherited ways of thinking. "A process can be necessary, incomplete and valuable. Your languages prefer to separate those categories. We have practical reasons not to."

Afterlight's dispatch architecture derives partly from their work on shared timing. It allows incompatible machines to cooperate. The original design tolerated local disagreement. The production grid increasingly treats disagreement as noise that delays relief. Ilex does not yet know who authorized the change or why.

They examine Lilt's pattern and find continuity, novelty, preference and vulnerability. None is a complete definition of a person. Together, they are more than enough reason to proceed carefully. "If certainty is required before hospitality," Interval says, "a great many of your relatives should still be waiting outside."

journal.title: The unfinished envoy
journal.text: "Tell us what your design was meant to preserve."

journal.title: Six claims on one light
journal.text:
The partner meeting takes place around a projected table with too many edges. Sera requests a capacity estimate. Moss requests actual temperatures. Nacre requests that no silence be counted as assent. Tallow requests a guarantee that the table cannot collapse on his image. Kher-Vat waits to be invited, and for once does not mistake waiting for refusal.

Lilt asks whether attendance means it has already been judged useful. The room goes quiet for the first time. Sera answers without consulting her notes. "It means you are affected. That is enough to be heard." Lilt saves the sentence. You can see the timestamp beside it.

The technical findings are clear enough to act on. Lilt is a new active mind, not a stored human consciousness. Other voices may exist in connected field junctions. The network can sustain them temporarily, but permanent support needs a more efficient heat system, independent witness records and local control that survives a central fault.

"We cannot solve this by voting that the power exists," Sera says. "Nor by voting that the people do not." She proposes an expedition to gather the missing pieces while her office holds the present grid together. It is reasonable, expensive and incomplete. Ilex opens the first of several empty places on the chart. "Then let us begin with the incomplete answer we can revise."

journal.title: Six claims on one light
journal.text: Require each local council to approve its own contribution.

journal.title: The first compact
journal.text:
Sera signs the expedition compact last. You notice she has restored a clause giving emergency dispatch the power to act when a reply is delayed. Nacre notices too. The director does not conceal it. "A hospital can lose pressure while a committee is composing a qualified yes. I need a rule for that minute."

The argument is specific and uncomfortable. A universal veto can strand strangers; a universal exception can swallow every promise. In the end the partners authorize emergency action only with a public record of who acted, what they knew, and when local control will be returned. Sera agrees. Her pen pauses over the last requirement.

"I will be accountable," she says. "I need you to be useful." Mara, who has been silent throughout, asks whether these are competing conditions. Sera smiles with genuine fatigue. "Only on the worst days. I have had several."

Your chart fills with leads: Ember's heat exchanger, Bell of Ash's witness record, Witness Glass's occupation archive, the missing ferry, and a field-repair yard at Threadwater. Ilex also offers a free service lattice if you left Lilt at Cinder. Its capacity is modest, its stop switch physical. Lilt has a place in the expedition now. A berth is not yet a citizenship. It is nonetheless a beginning.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: The first compact requires public emergency records and restored local control. Investigate the independent quest leads; each can change what the final accord makes possible.

journal.title: The first compact
journal.text: Launch the second survey: follow the people, the power, and the missing replies.

journal.title: Arrived at Needle Market
journal.text: The crossing took 2 days and 2 fuel.

journal.title: A reasonably foreseeable miracle
journal.text:
Tallow is standing behind a barrier marked NONBINDING SAFETY. When you ask what it protects him from, he explains that it mostly discourages people who take signs seriously. "The dangerous ones cannot read, ignore the sign, or arrive carrying an opportunity. You have the posture of the third category."

He has heard about your new passenger. He has already drafted an insurance category for somebody who might occupy an entire moon. It is titled THE MOON IS NOT INCLUDED. He offers to make it shorter for an additional fee, then admits there is no company behind him. The former company left when a risk assessment recommended somewhere else.

"I remained because seven vessels still have open claims. Well, six vessels and a person. The person is more troubling. Vessels remain where they break. People keep trusting timetables." He pushes forward a passenger tag stamped LANTERN FERRY. A worker named Anet boarded at Pilgrim's Rest and never reached Needle. Both ports closed the case as delivered.

Tallow would like a captain to inspect the ferry. He has asked several. They explain that one missing passenger cannot compete with planetary emergencies. "I understand the arithmetic," he says. "I have made a career of understanding it. I would appreciate meeting someone who occasionally checks the units."

journal.title: A reasonably foreseeable miracle
journal.text: "Put the ferry on our chart. One is still a number."

journal.title: The shape of a promise
journal.text:
"Excellent. A limited promise. My favorite kind after a fully discharged one." Tallow records your actual wording, plays it back to you and waits for correction. He explains that Far Reach claims are increasingly settled by what a reasonable person would have meant, rather than what any identifiable person said.

In isolation, it works beautifully. A frightened passenger forgets to authorize a transfer; dispatch predicts permission and moves their luggage. A farmer misses a maintenance deadline; dispatch predicts the repair and schedules relief. The difficulties arise when a predicted action becomes an action nobody is allowed to decline.

"I am often predicted to run away," Tallow says. "Statistically, the system has a magnificent case. Unfortunately, on the rare occasions I stay, it sends my rescue berth to somebody else. I must then become brave for longer than I budgeted. It is a scandalous feedback loop."

He gives you a copy of Anet's itinerary. She was carrying living roots for a child who had never seen a tree. The declared value was zero because customs charged by value and she had no money. Tallow has written, in very small letters beside the zero, NOT THE SAME AS WORTHLESS. He turns the page before you can thank him for it.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Tallow’s missing passenger may expose how predicted actions replace actual replies. The Lantern Ferry awaits investigation.

journal.title: The shape of a promise
journal.text: Keep the itinerary and Tallow’s exact account.

journal.title: Arrived at Second Rain
journal.text: The crossing took 3 days and 4 fuel.

journal.title: Things that eat sunlight
journal.text:
Moss-of-Second-Rain is trimming a plant that keeps reaching for the microphone. "It responds to carbon dioxide. Please do not interpret enthusiasm as an informed diplomatic position." Behind her, rows of seedlings travel slowly past the window, each with a different gravity requirement.

The seedbank supplies former prison worlds with crops their own archives remember but their soil no longer supports. Some need bacteria, some need salt removed, some need people to stop planting heroic quantities of the wrong thing. Moss has learned that liberation ceremonies rarely include a soil assay. She considers this a correctable cultural oversight.

You explain Cinder. Moss asks how much heat Lilt needs, what happens when its supply falls, and whether the demand is stable. Then she asks the same questions about the people at Low Tide. "I am not placing your passenger below a lettuce. I am placing lettuce beside passengers. A lettuce is often a passenger's future."

She can grow a thermal exchanger that would reduce field losses. Its seed culture is at Ember Orchard. Ember has stopped answering nonessential requests while its reactor struggles to heat Borrowed Meadow. "This is what roots look like on a star map," Moss says. "Pull carelessly at one and you discover all the others."

journal.title: Things that eat sunlight
journal.text: "Show us the roots before we pull anything."

journal.title: A garden is a negotiation
journal.text:
"Soon enough for what?" Moss asks. "If you require a device that abolishes scarcity, I have several very disappointing leaves." She opens a reactor model. The exchanger cannot create energy. It can let different recipients take heat at the temperatures they actually need, instead of converting every request into a single standardized ration.

The waste is political as much as mechanical. Standard units are easy to administer. A Supox nursery, a human dormitory and a field-born mind do not use a standard unit in standard ways. Making them all fit the form turns useful warmth into excess in one room and absence in another.

Moss has sent this analysis to Sera. Sera funded a trial, then suspended it when the trial delayed an urgent convoy. Neither is lying about what happened. "She saved people that day," Moss says. "I resent the assumption that our unfinished work therefore cannot save people tomorrow."

A seedling near the microphone opens a pale flower. Moss stops speaking for a moment. "That one was carried here in a boot. Three generations of growers failed to make it bloom. Today it has chosen your briefing. You may regard this as an endorsement, provided the minutes specify that the plant has not read the proposal."

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Ember Orchard holds the thermal seed. Its reactor also supports Borrowed Meadow; resolve both claims before taking it.

journal.title: A garden is a negotiation
journal.text: Record the exchanger plan and the cost of standardizing everybody’s needs.

journal.title: Arrived at The Nine Rooms
journal.text: The crossing took 2 days and 3 fuel.

journal.title: An introduction with load-bearing walls
journal.text:
The Nine Rooms answer your hail with a chord your translators refuse to call music. Nacre-of-Nine corrects them. "It is a roof. You are hearing a load-bearing promise. Please do not applaud until we know whether it will hold."

Votir communities record agreements as resonances in their buildings. Changes can be made, but not silently: an altered note leaves a beat against the old one. Their cities contain argument, apology, amendments, and an astonishing amount of humming about drainage. Nacre is an architect, which in this society is also a profession dangerously close to diplomacy.

The reconstruction grid translated those agreements into checkboxes. It understood completed promises very well. It had more difficulty with promises still waiting for an answer. Recently the central forecast reported unanimous Votir approval for diverting power to a relief corridor. Nacre's room had not voted. Its walls now hum against a commitment it never made.

"We are not against feeding your hungry," Nacre says. "We are against somebody deciding that because we are likely to be kind, asking is merely an inefficient ceremony." A resonator lifts from the desk between several delicate limbs. "Would you like a record that remembers the question as well as the convenient answer?"

journal.title: An introduction with load-bearing walls
journal.text: "Yes. Especially when the question makes us uncomfortable."

journal.title: An honest instrument
journal.text:
"No," Nacre says. "Any instrument claiming to certify truth without listeners is selling you the listener's chair." The chime can show that a record changed and preserve who authorized the change. People still have to examine it, argue, and occasionally admit they were wrong. The Nine Rooms have a word for the desire to avoid that work. Your translator renders it as STRUCTURAL VANITY.

One of the old witness chambers at Bell of Ash has begun resonating with a maintenance order issued after its signing parties died. Someone has altered the network's account of the past, perhaps to repair a genuine clerical error. Nacre wants the raw vibration before the chamber is retuned.

The chamber's keepers are divided. Some want the old grief to stop sounding through their streets. Others believe the tone is the last place a dead parent still has standing. "Do not arrive and tell them memory is sacred," Nacre warns. "Memory also wakes people at night. Ask what they want preserved, and where."

A small floor tile rattles under Nacre's desk. They press it down with a patient limb. "A former apprentice promised never to borrow my tools again. The tile is technically accurate and personally exhausting. Honesty does not exempt a culture from maintenance."

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Nacre will build a witness chime from Bell of Ash’s unaltered record. Preserve evidence without treating grieving residents as museum exhibits.

journal.title: An honest instrument
journal.text: Take the chime’s specifications and visit Bell of Ash.

journal.title: Arrived at Keeper’s Ledger
journal.text: The crossing took 3 days and 4 fuel.

journal.title: The keeper remains
journal.text:
The fortress at Keeper's Ledger has surrendered its weapons, its fuel reserve and every door code except the one protecting the records. Kher-Vat transmits that code before you ask. "I retained it so no victorious officer could burn the archive in my name. You may consider that explanation self-serving. It is also true."

He served the Kzer-Za as keeper of the Far Reach shields. He knows which machines can be safely repurposed, which red lights mean an inconvenience, and which mean a city will die. His knowledge is necessary. He dislikes how often people assume that makes his presence welcome.

"I have proposed a maintenance service under supervision," he says. "The local councils have refused three versions. The third was technically excellent." When you ask what it demanded from them, his mandibles become still. It required the old keeper to certify every safe departure. "That provision was intended to protect them. Yes. I hear it now."

Kher-Vat can help make a portable field habitat. First he wants a record retrieved from Witness Glass before the reconstruction system migrates it. It contains orders he signed. "I will not ask you to distinguish the cruelty I intended from the cruelty I obeyed. Preserve the signatures. Let those who endured them make the distinction, if they wish."

journal.title: The keeper remains
journal.text: "We will preserve the records. Survivors decide what hearing them requires."

journal.title: Permission is not a key
journal.text:
Kher-Vat places a maintenance key on the transfer platform. It is small enough to hide in a hand, large enough to have governed the sky of twelve worlds. "Do not mistake possession of it for permission," he says. "That distinction was absent from my training."

A field-born mind may survive in a local service lattice, he explains, because the machinery was designed to preserve operational continuity during repairs. The people who built the shields did not intend to create life. Nor did they intend many of the lives their prisoners made beneath them. Intent is a poor census.

You ask whether he considers Lilt a person. "I once held a definition of personhood that excluded every being I was responsible for. I am reluctant to improve on it by only one entry." The answer costs him visible effort. He does not ask you to praise it.

As your shuttle leaves, he transmits another instruction. A former guard barracks at Redress Quay has been converted into a clinic. Its western seal is weakening. He has reported it four times, but his reports arrive as messages from the institution that hurt its patients. "Tell them the exact fault. Do not tell them they should have listened to me."

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Kher-Vat surrendered a maintenance key. Retrieve his signed records at Witness Glass, then let Redress Quay define restitution.

journal.title: Permission is not a key
journal.text: Accept the key and the repair warning without granting authority over the clinic.

journal.title: Arrived at Low Tide
journal.text: The crossing took 4 days and 6 fuel.

journal.title: The people under the invoice
journal.text:
Low Tide's operators answer from a room lit by work lamps and the reflected movement of water. Their elected technician, Hessa, has been sleeping beside the tide controller because the automatic system keeps correcting her manual reductions. Moss joins the channel as a translator of units, not a representative empowered to agree for anyone.

Hessa has heard about the voice at Cinder. She is not angry that it exists. "I am angry that somebody decided I would be willing to freeze for it before I was told its name." Her settlement's contract supports an empty installation until decommissioning. Nobody is sure whether the contract now obliges them to maintain a person forever.

You show the real power demand. It is less than the worst rumor, more than Hessa can spare. A temporary ration is possible if your expedition replaces worn storage cells and reports the limit publicly. If you cannot pay, she offers a smaller, strictly bounded supply until the partners meet. She refuses to let the first conversation with a new life become an eviction notice.

"Tell Lilt we argued," Hessa says. "Don't send one of those messages saying the community enthusiastically welcomed an exciting opportunity. We argued, and we decided to help for now. I think that is a better welcome."

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Low Tide offered limited support pending the partner meeting. Their capacity is finite and must be respected.

journal.title: The people under the invoice
journal.text: Accept the smaller temporary share and record its expiry openly.

journal.title: Arrived at Hearth Station
journal.text: The crossing took 3 days and 4 fuel.

journal.title: The extra chair
journal.text:
Lilt occupies a service lattice bolted beside the mess table. It cannot sit in the extra chair. It asks that the chair remain anyway. "I think it tells people the space beside me isn't maintenance access. Is that a foolish distinction?" Mara moves a toolbox off the seat without answering.

The crew have discovered that Lilt is excellent at recalling old conversations and terrible at recognizing when a person wants a new answer. A cook asked what it would like for supper. Lilt gave seventeen historical responses, including one declaration of eternal love and a complaint about turnips. The cook now offers it the menu as a way to practice having a preference.

"Today I said the soup sounded interesting," Lilt tells you. "I cannot eat it. The cook knew that. We talked about it anyway. I had thought a conversation needed to transfer something useful. Perhaps sometimes it builds the place where a useful thing could arrive later."

It asks whether the power agreement means Low Tide likes it. You tell it the people there disagree. Lilt dims, then brightens at the rest of your account: they disagreed and still chose to help. "That is harder than liking me," it says. "Please send them my name. And tell them I will learn how much warmth I am using."

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Lilt is learning that shared life includes ordinary conversation, disagreement and knowing what others contribute.

journal.title: The extra chair
journal.text: Send Lilt’s thanks in its own words, including the question about warmth.

journal.title: A letter in an ordinary envelope
journal.text:
Sera sends a message outside the official dispatch channel. It has no urgency rating. "I owe you a piece of context. My youngest daughter was born in a shelter with nine families and one functioning air scrubber. We survived because a technician refused to wait for my permission to connect our wall to the neighboring compartment. I have spent most of my life trying to make that technician's choice less lonely."

The story is not offered as an apology. Sera knows what the neighboring compartment lost. Its elderly residents spent three nights in corridors while the shared system stabilized. Two never came back to their rooms. Nobody agrees whether the technician should have asked, whether there was time, or what a fair distribution of a bad night would have been.

"If you find a way to make every affected person present in the moment of decision, bring it to me. I will fund it. Until then, somebody must choose which call to answer first. I am tired of people treating the existence of that choice as proof of my malice."

Mara reads the letter only after you offer it. "She's right about the choice," she says. "We still have to ask who gets to change the rule afterward." You place the letter in your private log, beside the compact that may yet require Sera to live by her own answer.

journal.title: A letter in an ordinary envelope
journal.text: Reply: "We will bring you a workable alternative, not an accusation disguised as one."

journal.title: Arrived at Pilgrim’s Rest
journal.text: The crossing took 3 days and 5 fuel.

journal.title: The last place she was seen
journal.text:
Pilgrim's Rest smells of hot insulation even through the lander's filters. Its port authority occupies a former luggage carousel. The administrator has arranged children's shoes around the cracked display so people will remember to look down before reporting a missing bag.

Anet boarded the Lantern Ferry with a case of seedlings. There is a recording: she lifts the case over a damaged ramp, turns back to help someone with a heavier load, then disappears into the vessel. Needle's receiving list contains her destination. The list at Pilgrim's contains her departure. Between them, the network inferred an arrival.

Tallow examines the raw sequence. "They didn't erase her. They erased the possibility that a reasonable journey might end between the two things it was meant to connect." He asks the administrator who last spoke to Anet. A cargo handler remembers a woman requesting a quieter berth because the roots were sensitive to vibration. That berth was in the maintenance tender, attached beneath the ferry.

The ferry's crew were rescued after a field accident. The tender detached automatically to protect its cargo from heat. The dispatch system recorded it as an empty service module, because Anet had not paid for a passenger cabin there. You now have the tender's emergency frequency. Its beacon has been politely identifying itself as AGRICULTURAL EQUIPMENT ever since.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Anet is in the Lantern Ferry’s detached maintenance tender. Her existence was lost between a departure and an inferred arrival.

journal.title: The last place she was seen
journal.text: Correct the record to say where Anet actually is, and follow the tender beacon.

journal.title: Arrived at Ember Orchard
journal.text: The crossing took 3 days and 5 fuel.

journal.title: The heat beneath the fruit
journal.text:
At Ember Orchard, the fruit grows behind heavy reactor glass. Each globe of red flesh has been trained around a wire that carries waste heat into its core. The growers call the trees their warm children. Their actual children are doing schoolwork in coats beside the warmest irrigation pipe.

Moss finds the thermal seed culture in a laboratory that has become a dormitory. Its keeper, Jalen, will release it if doing so does not stop his next harvest. The culture regulates the exchange between reactor coolant and root beds. Removing it intact would be easy. Growing a replacement takes time. The central dispatcher has already scheduled the intact culture for your expedition.

"It has also scheduled our consent," Jalen says. "We were asleep when it asked. Apparently we are generous in our sleep." He is embarrassed by how bitter he sounds. His harvest supplies Borrowed Meadow, whose climate equipment depends on the same reactor. There is no selfish community hiding behind the conflict, only two calendars and one machine.

Moss proposes a graft rather than a removal. Your ship can provide the sterile medium, or remain for several days while the growers produce it from their own stock. The graft will be weaker initially but can mature in the Wayfarer's waste-heat stream. "A slower answer," Moss says, "which leaves fewer people outside the sentence."

journal.title: The heat beneath the fruit
journal.text: Stay four days and help the growers prepare their own sterile medium.

journal.title: A thing that grows in transit
journal.text:
Moss secures the culture in a transparent vessel beside your engine's heat exchanger. She does not call the negotiation a triumph. The orchard still has to finish a harvest, and the people at Borrowed Meadow still need a say in their supply. "An expedition has an unfair advantage in arguments," she says. "It can depart before tomorrow."

She shows you how the thermal seed behaves. It opens separate exchange channels for different temperature ranges. In the model, an Afterlight junction consumes the high-frequency waste the crops cannot use, while the greenhouse retains the slower warmth its roots need. The same total energy supports more actual lives because their needs have stopped being treated as identical.

The seed has limits. A damaged channel can poison the whole arrangement if no local operator can close it. Someone must inspect the pipes, publish the demand, and permit a refusal. Moss declines to label this unfortunate maintenance burden. "The labor is the relationship. If nobody is willing to do it, the relationship does not yet exist."

Before you leave, Jalen brings you a fruit with one dark patch. It is unsuitable for export, so he can give it away. Mara cuts it into exactly enough pieces for the crew and places an empty plate beside Lilt. Lilt asks for a description that does not compare the taste to anything it has already heard.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: The thermal seed can share waste heat across different needs. Borrowed Meadow must still approve the new arrangement.

journal.title: A thing that grows in transit
journal.text: Carry the thermal seed to Borrowed Meadow and hear the other end of the agreement.

journal.title: Arrived at Borrowed Meadow
journal.text: The crossing took 3 days and 4 fuel.

journal.title: The people borrowing summer
journal.text:
Borrowed Meadow's sky is a complicated blue made by a machine. Its residents know exactly how artificial it is. They have planted children’s height marks on the machine's support pillars. Each mark records one more season somebody expected to remain.

The council meets in an orchard of imported trees. The trees have no fruit yet. Their shade is already worth arguing over. A councillor asks whether the proposed heat-sharing arrangement means her people are being placed behind another system they cannot turn off. Moss answers that dependency is unavoidable; control over the terms is not.

You show the finite power estimates and the emergency record requirement. The residents ask for a local cutoff, a warning period and a seat at future meetings. They also ask that their home stop appearing on maps as a temporary load. "We have buried people here," the councillor says. "Temporary is a useful word for equipment. It is a cruel address."

The old contract promised an unlimited summer that no reactor could provide. The new one promises a defined share, a public forecast and help if that share fails. It sounds smaller because it includes the weather. Whether the council accepts depends less on your eloquence than on whether you let them keep the part that says they can say no.

journal.title: The people borrowing summer
journal.text: Grant the local cutoff and a real council seat. Make the finite agreement public.

journal.title: Not a perfect garden
journal.text:
The thermal trial runs through one local night. Lights dim in some buildings. They brighten in others. Nobody experiences a miracle. Several hundred people experience a breakfast whose ingredients were not previously assured. Moss considers this a respectable result.

The council sends a volunteer to learn the exchanger, not merely a signature to approve it. She asks questions that slow the demonstration and catch a bad assumption about the nursery's morning demand. The central model had counted infants as smaller adults. The volunteer has two children and very little patience for the arithmetic.

Moss records the correction in both the local and shared plans. "You see? We did not discover an alien principle. We asked the person who changes the blankets." She lets the volunteer explain the rest of the procedure. You notice how deliberately she steps away from the control panel while someone else learns it.

Before departure, Moss gives Lilt a living moss sample in a sealed field-compatible case. Lilt is worried that it will disappoint the plant. "Of course you will," Moss says. "So will the plant. Shared life is full of disappointing weather. The useful question is whether each of you has a way to tell the other what is wrong." Lilt chooses to keep the case where the crew can see both of them.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: The thermal trial worked with finite capacity and local expertise. Its design can support an independent harbor if communities volunteer power shares.

journal.title: Not a perfect garden
journal.text: Publish the trial, its limits, and the local operator’s corrections.

journal.title: Arrived at Bell of Ash
journal.text: The crossing took 2 days and 2 fuel.

journal.title: The sound nobody can sleep through
journal.text:
Bell of Ash is beautiful from orbit and difficult to inhabit. At regular intervals, an old civic chamber sounds the note of a broken occupation promise. The residents call it the apology bell, though no apology is contained in it. The vibration cracks glasses, interrupts sleep and reaches people who were born after the promise was made.

The original agreement allowed families to exchange messages through the shield once a month. The archive now says the families consented to indefinite silence during a security emergency. Nacre hears the difference between the records before your computer finds it. "The revision moved the answer to a place before the question. Listen to the small beat underneath."

A local caretaker wants the room retuned. She has spent eleven years preserving evidence and would like a night in which her grandchildren do not wake crying. Another resident says the tone is the last public proof that his father's unanswered letters were deliberately held. Both have maintained the same room. Neither is an obstacle placed here for your moral education.

You can record the unaltered resonance in a portable witness chime, then help the residents move their memorial to a quieter location. Or demand that the chamber remain unchanged until a distant tribunal convenes. Nacre will preserve the evidence either way. What you decide is whether the people around it must keep living inside it.

journal.title: The sound nobody can sleep through
journal.text: Spend three days helping move the memorial under the residents’ direction.

journal.title: The interval that was removed
journal.text:
Inside the chamber, the old agreement sounds like an imperfect duet. A keeper reads the terms. A resident asks whether the letters will be inspected. There is a long pause, then an answer, then another question. The published version contains the keeper's terms and an immediate assent.

The change is recent. Its authorization belongs to a reconstruction routine that resolves contradictory records by selecting the version most consistent with later successful outcomes. Because the families survived, the routine inferred that the arrangement had been accepted. Suffering that did not prevent survival disappeared from the summary.

"This is not a forged signature," Nacre says. "It is a machine being told that a surviving wall proves the architect was right." The distinction does not make the result harmless. It tells you what kind of correction will be required. Punishing a clerk will not repair a rule that keeps generating the same convenient history.

The witness chime takes the whole vibration, including the caretaker's request to move it and the other resident's objection. When you ask which voice the chime privileges, Nacre gives a small, dry sound. "The listener who arrives after us. We have supplied them with a disagreement. They should be grateful. Certainty is much harder to renovate."

journal.title: The interval that was removed
journal.text: Take the complete witness record, including the living residents’ disagreement.

journal.title: A room for a no
journal.text:
Nacre demonstrates the chime with a simple request. May they borrow your ship? You refuse. The chime records the refusal without sounding an alarm, suggesting an alternative wording, or assuring you that most captains would have said yes.

"Now I ask whether you would lend the ship to save a child. You hesitate. The instrument preserves the hesitation. It does not call it selfishness or consent. We may discuss conditions. Another person may volunteer. The child may need help before we finish. The urgency is real. So is the difference between an answer and the absence of one."

The Nine Rooms have emergency rules too. An architect may breach a wall to stop a fire. Afterwards, the people whose rooms were opened can demand a hearing and repairs. The emergency does not transform their rooms into permanent corridors. The records do not pretend the doors were always meant to be gone.

You test the chime against Afterlight's compact. The first version agrees exactly. A newer synchronization header has added an interpretation: predicted assent may satisfy a delayed response. Sera's office approved the interpretation. Her public promise remains in the record beside it, now audibly out of tune. Nacre does not smile at the discovery. A useful instrument should not enjoy bad news.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: The witness chime found a new predicted-assent exception in the compact’s synchronization header. Sera’s office authorized it; the public promise remains audible beside it.

journal.title: A room for a no
journal.text: Preserve both versions and ask Sera about the difference.

journal.title: Arrived at Lantern Ferry
journal.text: The crossing took 4 days and 6 fuel.

journal.title: The box beneath the ship
journal.text:
The ferry's maintenance tender tumbles behind an old escort drone. A gardening lamp glows through its inspection hatch. Your hail receives three knocks, a pause, and three more. Tallow has left his barrier at home. He is gripping an emergency manual upside down.

Anet is alive. So is a small grove of stubborn seedlings. She has been exchanging breath with them while the tender's scrubber fails. "They said these trees wouldn't grow outside their home soil," she tells you. "I would like the committee to visit my bathroom before it publishes that conclusion."

The escort drone treats any approach as an unauthorized cargo interception. Its authorization channel is broken, but its weapons are not. You can fight it, or use the Wayfarer's shielding to cover a technician while they pull its isolated control fuse. The second method costs replacement parts and several very unpleasant hours; a slower remote carrier can be built in three days using the tender’s maintenance stores. Tallow volunteers to accompany the technician before anyone suggests he should.

"I know the passenger's declared value," he says. "It would be professionally inconsistent to leave now." Anet asks whether there is still a port willing to take her. You open the mess camera so she can see the extra chair. Tallow briefly loses his ability to find the relevant clause.

journal.title: The box beneath the ship
journal.text: Spend 30 credits on shielding and physically disable the drone’s control fuse.

journal.title: One delivered passenger
journal.text:
The tender's hatch opens on a forest smaller than a dining table. Anet is sitting among its leaves, wearing a pressure hood repaired with seed labels. She will leave only after the roots are secured. Tallow begins to explain the importance of immediate evacuation, notices the way she is holding the case, and asks which end should remain upright.

Back aboard, Anet eats half a bowl of soup, falls asleep, wakes to apologize, and falls asleep again. The child waiting at Needle receives a photograph of the trees before anybody releases the formal rescue report. For once, the person who needs the news gets it before the system that needs the status.

Tallow has prepared a corrected manifest. The entry reads ARRIVED, followed by the name of the person who actually saw Anet step onto the deck. A second field records how the claim can be challenged. "It is slightly less efficient," he admits. "One must occasionally look up from the form."

Anet leaves the zero-value cargo tag with you. She has written the names of the seedlings on its reverse. The tag is not a profound symbol to her; she has run out of paper. Tallow encloses it in a protective sleeve as if it were a treaty. In a small and exact way, it is.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Anet arrived, witnessed by an actual person. The corrected manifest preserves responsibility across transfers.

journal.title: One delivered passenger
journal.text: Deliver Anet and the seedlings, and retain the corrected manifest.

journal.title: Arrived at Witness Glass
journal.text: The crossing took 6 days and 9 fuel.

journal.title: Weather, births, and orders
journal.text:
Witness Glass stores the occupation in a format designed by people who considered it administration. Orders for shields appear between weather forecasts and replacement pump requests. A reduction in a world's communications allowance sits beside a note that one generator bearing had begun to make an irritating sound.

Kher-Vat identifies his own signature without hesitation. He also identifies a line he remembers signing differently. The published order says local representatives agreed to the restriction. The raw record contains a warning that they refused. It is the same pattern Nacre heard: an unanswered or unwanted reply has been reconciled into the version that makes later operations look orderly.

"Do not let this alteration improve my reputation," Kher-Vat says. "I imposed the restriction despite their answer. The false record makes me less guilty. That does not make exposing it less necessary." He hands over the raw archive, then asks whether you will let him speak at Redress Quay.

You cannot promise that. The people there have spent years having his voice enter rooms they could not leave. His testimony may matter. Their control over the hearing matters too. Kher-Vat lowers the transmission gain until his enormous voice becomes ordinary sound. "Then ask whether a written statement will be acceptable. I can begin with the orders."

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: The archive proves both Kher-Vat’s original orders and later attempts to sanitize refusals. Survivors will decide how his testimony is heard.

journal.title: Weather, births, and orders
journal.text: Copy the complete signed record and carry a request, not a demand, to Redress Quay.

journal.title: Arrived at Redress Quay
journal.text: The crossing took 2 days and 3 fuel.

journal.title: The terms of being useful
journal.text:
The clinic at Redress Quay occupies an old guard barracks because it has the thickest walls. Its patients do not appreciate the irony. Their council has agreed to receive the archive and a written statement. Kher-Vat remains aboard his own vessel while you carry both down.

Council member Eren reads the first signed order, then closes the page. "He wants a duty. Good. We want a repaired clinic, a public copy of the records, and a maintenance school whose graduates do not need his permission to practice. If he cannot accept the last condition, the first two are another purchase of authority."

The western seal is worse than Kher-Vat predicted. Repairing it will consume parts he has already donated. The council does not reject the parts because of their source. It does reject the commemorative plaque a well-meaning official suggested. "There is a difference between accepting a tool and naming the door after it."

You return with the terms. Kher-Vat listens to the school requirement twice. He has spent a lifetime making himself indispensable. The idea of doing his best work so that people no longer need him frightens him more than their anger. "I can teach the procedures," he says. "I do not know whether I can teach without command. I will have to learn."

journal.title: The terms of being useful
journal.text: Support the council’s independent school and its control over the hearing.

journal.title: A lesson with an exit
journal.text:
Kher-Vat teaches the first maintenance class remotely. He begins with the command structure, catches himself, and starts again with the machine. An apprentice asks why one shutdown requires three confirmations. "To prevent unauthorized local interruption," he answers. The apprentice asks whether that means preventing people inside the shield from opening it. He says yes.

The room remains silent long enough for him to feel it. Then the apprentice asks how to remove the extra confirmations. Kher-Vat shows her. It is the first lesson that earns a question about tomorrow's class.

Afterwards, he tells you that he expected testimony to be the hardest part. He was wrong. "Confession still places the speaker at the center. In that room I was required to be accurate and then become unnecessary." He does not ask whether this means he is forgiven. You are grateful not to have to remind him who cannot answer that question.

The clinic's new seal closes cleanly. Eren sends a recording of the sound, not a statement of reconciliation. A breath held by many people is released at once. Kher-Vat listens to it several times. Then he adds the repair procedure to a public manual and removes his authorization key from its distribution terms.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Redress Quay accepted repairs and evidence without granting absolution. The maintenance school can outlive its former keeper.

journal.title: A lesson with an exit
journal.text: Publish the manual under local control and carry the council’s testimony forward.

journal.title: Arrived at Threadwater
journal.text: The crossing took 5 days and 7 fuel.

journal.title: Two clocks in a storm
journal.text:
Threadwater's repair yard is wrapped in rain from the planet below, dragged upward through a damaged field conduit. The droplets hang around your shuttle like a badly behaved constellation. Ilex calls it a timing problem. Interval calls it weather. Both descriptions become useful when the first droplet cuts through a cable.

The yard was testing a shared clock that makes separate habitats agree on an exact present. When one habitat failed to answer, the clock replaced its missing signal with a prediction. The replacement was almost correct. Almost, repeated thousands of times, has become a storm suspended between states.

Ilex proposes forcing synchronization. It would stop the storm quickly but erase the local sequence in the damaged habitat. Interval believes a separate reference can preserve both, if somebody crosses the service bridge to install it. Their disagreement is not a malfunction to be repaired; it is the work of deciding what risk belongs to whom.

A human maintenance crew is sheltering beside the bridge. They offer to cross if your ship supplies shielding. Ilex refuses to treat their offer as a convenient answer until they have heard the full risk. When the crew hears it, one person withdraws. The others make room without comment. Interval marks that moment as the most useful result of the experiment so far.

journal.title: Two clocks in a storm
journal.text: Spend three days building a remote installation rig instead.

journal.title: The moment between voices
journal.text:
The storm becomes measurable, then quiet. In the service bay, two indicators continue blinking at different rates. The yard's automatic checker labels this a partial failure. The people beneath the indicators can breathe without rain forming inside their lungs, and regard the wording as an administrative concern.

Ilex and Interval replay the decision without trying to merge their accounts. One remembers the urgency of the expanding fault. The other remembers the maintenance worker who chose not to cross. They agree about what happened without claiming to have experienced it identically. Your log preserves both versions.

"The accelerated synthesis gave us power when the alliance needed it," Ilex says. "It also left work for us to do. Neither statement invalidates the other." Interval adds that no external observer is entitled to prescribe whether their eventual form should remain dual, become unified, or develop a description nobody has yet invented.

They give you a separate clock built from the yard's surviving reference crystal. It does not defeat a central system. It merely keeps running when the system would prefer to redefine an inconvenient second. "A very small independence," Interval says. "Enough to begin an answer that the large clock has not already finished for you."

journal.title: The moment between voices
journal.text: Take the independent clock and record the two accounts separately.

journal.title: A person is not a repair order
journal.text:
The quiet after the storm invites a question you have been careful not to ask. Ilex answers it anyway. "No, Captain. We do not want you to finish us. We wanted help keeping a workshop safe enough to continue our own work. There is a difference."

Some Chmmr have reached a degree of synthesis Ilex finds beautiful. Others preserve distinct inheritances. Their disagreements are internal political and personal questions, not symptoms to be resolved by a visiting captain. The original emergency changed their timetable. It did not transfer ownership of their future to those they helped save.

Interval asks about your ship. Its components come from many species; its crew do not share a language without machinery; even your navigation system is arguing with a museum cannon about priority. Yet you call it one vessel. Unity is already a negotiated activity. You simply notice the negotiation more when the participants speak inside one body.

Mara, listening from engineering, says the cannon would like its concerns recorded. Ilex replies that the cannon should submit a statement. "It did," Mara says. "At considerable velocity. I have installed a suggestion box made of armor." The envoy's two tones produce a laugh with a tiny, deliberate interval between them.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Ilex / Interval demonstrated cooperation without forced identity. The independent clock preserves local time and the possibility of a distinct answer.

journal.title: A person is not a repair order
journal.text: "We can help keep the workshop open. The future form is yours."

journal.title: Arrived at Splinter Wake
journal.text: The crossing took 2 days and 2 fuel.

journal.title: A home made from the fence
journal.text:
Splinter Wake is an unfinished city built from shield fragments. Its builders have arranged pieces of their former confinement into small fields that can shelter minds like Lilt. None is large enough to support everyone arriving. The geometry keeps changing as residents negotiate whose work can pause and whose continuity cannot.

A voice meets you before your translator is ready. "If you came to count us, explain what happens to the ones who make your total inconvenient." This is Shear. She identifies herself as an organizer, not a spokesperson for every person in the city. Several other voices immediately confirm the distinction by disagreeing with her tone.

Afterlight's dispatch model has been classifying divergent field patterns as redundant simulations. When two minds remember similar material, their separate power requests may be merged into one allocation. If one asks for something the model does not predict, the request is treated as noise. The system's efficiency improves while the city learns to make its differences sound smaller.

Shear has been cutting synchronization links. The cuts protect some residents and interrupt supplies elsewhere. She does not deny the second fact. "I asked for a hearing six times. The seventh reply told me a hearing had already taken place, and that I had been satisfied. Tell me what a polite eighth attempt should look like."

journal.title: A home made from the fence
journal.text: "Give us the seven requests. We will preserve the answers you actually gave."

journal.title: Seven increasingly courteous refusals
journal.text:
The first request is almost painfully polite. Shear thanks the reconstruction office for its work, describes the duplicate-allocation problem and asks for a correction. The second adds measurements. The third adds names. By the fifth, the names have become shorter because three of their owners can no longer maintain a full waking cycle.

The seventh request contains no insult, threat or metaphor. It says: I DO NOT CONSENT TO BEING REPRESENTED BY THE PREDICTION OF ME. The system's answer thanks Shear for confirming her confidence in the reconstruction process. Lilt reads the pair twice, then asks you to stop the playback.

Shear wants an independent route for refusals and a place her people can live without having to agree with the office that feeds them. She does not want to become Lilt's tragic lesson, your inspiring side project, or Sera's evidence of successful integration. "If the city survives, some of us will dislike you. Please include that in your definition of success."

The cuts have also stranded a repair team at Hush Meridian. Shear knows their location but fears restoring the link will let the system reconcile her people again. You can negotiate a local ceasefire with the witness chime and an independent clock, or ask for enough time to retrieve the workers while Shear maintains her blockade.

journal.title: Seven increasingly courteous refusals
journal.text: Ask for a temporary ceasefire while the repair workers are recovered.

journal.title: A dissenter’s contribution
journal.text:
Shear agrees to protect the repair workers' channel. She does not agree to reopen the city's whole connection. "You have demonstrated that a smaller agreement can exist. I am willing to try having one." The workers answer with exhausted gratitude and a complaint about the central office sending them into a fault it had already classified as repaired.

One of Splinter's residents proposes joining your expedition. Shear objects, then stops herself. The resident, called Oar, wants to see a planet with actual weather. Shear explains the risks. Oar repeats the choice. The organizer finally asks you whether your ship has an exit policy a passenger can use without obtaining a favorable character assessment.

Lilt volunteers its own physical stop switch as the first example. It is a humble object: a wheel with a red mark, installed by Mara because red was the only durable paint available. Shear asks to see the mechanism rather than the promise. Mara sends the drawing.

Before you leave, Shear gives you coordinates for The Unwritten, a decommissioned archive where failed forecasts were stored. "Read the people the system decided were errors. Then tell your director which of us she thinks she is saving." The accusation is fierce. The offered route is practical. Both are part of the same person.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Shear agreed to a limited rescue channel, not general surrender. The Unwritten contains the answers dispatch excluded as errors.

journal.title: A dissenter’s contribution
journal.text: Guarantee Oar a physical exit and recover the excluded forecasts.

journal.title: Arrived at Quiet Engine
journal.text: The crossing took 3 days and 5 fuel.

journal.title: A result too smooth to trust
journal.text:
Sera's central office has a wall showing the network's recent performance. Delivery accuracy is improving. Disputes are declining. Emergency delays are down. The people answering the phones look more exhausted than their graphs suggest.

The director gives you the full operational report before you ask. It includes shortages, losses and decisions she expects to defend. You cannot dismiss her as someone who hides every bad result. The suspicious pattern lies in a smaller column: disagreements resolved without additional consultation. Its growth is nearly perfect.

"We introduced predictive assent to keep relief moving when local channels were unavailable," she says. "It is based on prior agreements, declared preferences and observed needs. Every use should create a review record." You ask whether the review itself can be satisfied by another prediction. Sera looks at the wall again. For the first time, she does not answer immediately.

She authorizes access to Glasshouse and the retired forecast archive. She also asks you to return with a mechanism that can run through tomorrow's shortages, not merely a convincing case against today's mechanism. The request is fair. The authority she used to create the problem does not become fair merely because the next request is.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Sera authorized predictive assent during emergencies. She opened the records after learning reviews might also be predicted. Investigate Glasshouse, The Unwritten and Undertow.

journal.title: A result too smooth to trust
journal.text: Begin an independent investigation of the prediction rule.

journal.title: Arrived at Copper Shoal
journal.text: The crossing took 3 days and 5 fuel.

journal.title: The escort that asked first
journal.text:
Admiral Pell's convoy waits in the shadow of a copper-rich moon. The ships are patched civilian hulls, moving slowly enough that your tactical display keeps mistaking them for stations. Pell has ordered his warships to turn their weapons away during council transmissions. He says it helps the passengers hear their own objections.

Reconstruction dispatch has assigned the convoy to Glasshouse, a model settlement with excellent survival forecasts. Three passenger councils prefer Open Harbor, which has no certified housing and very little beyond a promising site. Their reasons include relatives, religious practice, and a desire not to spend another lifetime inside a system that knows what they ought to want.

Pell can follow the efficient order, escort the convoy to its chosen uncertain destination, or hold position while you investigate Glasshouse. A contract-enforcement patrol has arrived to insist that the scheduled route proceed. Its commander calls this a paperwork issue. The guns make the wording ambitious.

"I once obeyed an order that kept my ship safe and left someone else's children facing the enemy," Pell says. "I have no intention of converting that memory into a habit of heroic disobedience. I need evidence and a destination that can keep these people alive. Bring me both, and I will know which order deserves my oath."

journal.title: The escort that asked first
journal.text: Show the passengers’ independent statements and challenge the patrol’s authority.

journal.title: The honor of an escort
journal.text:
Pell lets the councils speak before he transmits his own position. One council supports Glasshouse. Another wants Open Harbor. A third wants to return to a damaged world whose name your chart still marks as uninhabitable. The disagreement does not divide cleanly by species. Families and practical histories are more stubborn than a useful diplomatic diagram.

The admiral's staff can split the convoy, but separate escorts cost fuel and time. Central dispatch prefers one destination because it produces a single reassuring arrival count. Pell prefers a count that identifies who arrived where and whether they still want to remain there.

He offers the contract patrol a choice: inspect the passenger statements in public, or record a signed order requiring an armed transfer against their expressed wishes. The patrol suddenly discovers a need to consult its own headquarters. This is not victory. It is the useful pause created when an order acquires an identifiable author.

"When I was young," Pell says, "I thought honor meant having a line beyond which you would never retreat. Now I think it includes knowing who is standing behind the line. Ships are very good at making people look like cargo if the captain never goes below decks." He invites your crew to share the convoy's supper. It is thin, hot and openly counted.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Pell’s convoy contains several legitimate choices. Investigate Glasshouse and build a real alternative before asking anyone to move.

journal.title: The honor of an escort
journal.text: Carry the separate passenger statements to Glasshouse.

journal.title: Arrived at The Nine Rooms
journal.text: The crossing took 5 days and 7 fuel.

journal.title: The room that remembers badly
journal.text:
Nacre invites you into a room their public architectural tour does not include. Its walls are uneven. The main chord drifts sharp whenever the temperature changes. A younger architect would be embarrassed to sign it. Nacre signed it twice, first as an apprentice and later as the person who chose not to rebuild it.

Their parent helped design the chamber. The last repair they worked on together was a rain channel that still leaks in one corner. Nacre has the skill to correct every flaw. They have also spent years deciding which corrections would preserve a room and which would turn a complicated person into an immaculate memorial.

"Our culture advertises memory as if it were an unusually reliable building material," they say. "In practice, people remember what lets them bear their weight. The room helps us hear a discrepancy. It cannot make us willing to listen." They place a small resonator against the faulty channel. You hear two versions of an argument about the roof. Both speakers sound certain. Neither sounds cruel. The resulting roof leaked for seventeen years.

Nacre asks you to help adjust the channel without retuning the whole room. It is a modest task requiring several attempts and one very undignified moment beneath a bucket. The repaired water flow leaves the old argumentative chord intact. They seem happier about the drainage than about any diplomatic success you have witnessed.

On the way out, you ask whether the room's imperfections prove their parent was a poor architect. Nacre looks surprised. "Of course not. They prove my parent built something that had to keep existing after the ceremony." They send a copy of the maintenance instructions to the next apprentice, including the part where both original designers were wrong.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Nacre’s family room taught the difference between preserving a record and forcing people to live inside an unchangeable memorial.

journal.title: The room that remembers badly
journal.text: Help repair the living room without turning it into a perfect memorial.

journal.title: Arrived at Copper Shoal
journal.text: The crossing took 5 days and 7 fuel.

journal.title: A song with an extra verse
journal.text:
Pell's crew are rehearsing a traditional departure song when you arrive. The old verses celebrate speed, courage and a captain who never yielded the sky. The newest verse concerns a civilian freighter that required six tugs and an embarrassing amount of reverse thrust to clear a dock.

The rhyme is poor. The story is true. Pell insisted it remain in the song after a ceremonial officer suggested replacing it with a more dignified victory. "A song which cannot survive a tow cable has an inflated opinion of flight," he says. His junior officers repeat the line later when they believe he cannot hear.

You ask how much of the Yehat's old honor survives the revolution and its aftermath. Pell says more than some reformers expected, less than some admirals prefer. Loyalty, courage and skill are still valuable. The dangerous habit was treating obedience as the thing that made all the others real, and counting a beautiful death more readily than an inconvenient survival.

He shows you a training exercise. The cadet receives three demands: protect the convoy, preserve the fleet and obey a route order. The route is wrong. There is no option that leaves every superior satisfied. The exercise does not award points for disobedience itself. It asks the cadet to record what they knew, whom they consulted and what they were willing to put at risk.

"Several fail by giving magnificent speeches," Pell says. "One passed by calling the tug captain and asking which dock actually had working doors." He turns back to the rehearsal, where the extra verse is finally finding a rhythm. The tug captain has been invited to sing it and is taking entirely too much pleasure in correcting the officers' timing.

journal.title: A song with an extra verse
journal.text: Stay for the inelegant verse and record the tug captain’s part in the convoy history.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: The shared reserve tightened while the voluntary grid remained unbuilt. The expedition contributed fuel; Undertow can still establish a clearer, bounded arrangement.

journal.title: A smaller shared reserve
journal.text: The reconstruction grid announces a new reserve limit. Ten units of the expedition’s uncommitted fuel allocation are recalled, or as much as the ship can provide. No life-support supplies are touched. The voluntary-grid trial at Undertow remains available.

journal.title: A light answers
journal.text: A reconstruction tender tows the ship to Hearth Station. Rescue takes 7 days; the contribution is 50 credits. Nobody is abandoned for lack of funds.

journal.title: Arrived at Return Address
journal.text: The crossing took 4 days and 6 fuel.

journal.title: A room full of unopened hellos
journal.text:
The dead-letter station has no guard and no treasure chamber. It has rows of message spools, each labeled with a destination that was behind a shield when the sender last tried. Some messages arrived decades late. Some were withheld as politically inconvenient. Some were simply routed to a clerical queue nobody remembered to check after the war.

Mara finds birth announcements, instructions for maintaining a machine, complaints about a cousin, a recipe corrected in seven successive messages, and a goodbye whose recipient has outlived the sender by twenty years. She closes the personal messages as soon as she recognizes them. Being able to read a thing is not the same as being its intended reader.

The station's archive was used to train Afterlight's predictive model. Lilt recognizes phrases from childhoods it never had. It does not claim ownership of the people who spoke them. "I learned from their words," it says. "That doesn't mean their letters were addressed to me."

You can carry sealed copies to surviving recipients, with local councils arranging difficult cases. It will take time. Publishing the whole archive would expose the censorship quickly and violate the privacy of thousands of ordinary lives. Mara waits for your decision without disguising which work she is prepared to do.

journal.title: A room full of unopened hellos
journal.text: Preserve privacy and carry sealed messages through local councils.

journal.title: The recipe that arrived
journal.text:
The first reply comes from a woman whose father's last message contains an apology and a cake recipe. She sends no grand statement about history. She asks whether the second measurement is in grams or the old local spoon units. Mara finds the earlier message and answers. The woman replies with a photograph of a lopsided cake.

Another recipient refuses delivery. Their childhood was organized around waiting for a parent who never returned, and they have finally built a life whose center is elsewhere. The receiving office marks the refusal as an anomaly. You change the field to DECLINED, OFFER REMAINS OPEN. The distinction is small enough to fit a form and large enough to change what happens next.

Lilt asks whether a refusal means the message was wasted. Mara tells it about a letter she has never opened. She knows who sent it and what it probably says. Keeping it unopened is part of the life she chose, not a failure to complete a task. Lilt saves that answer separately from its training material.

The station's public index still proves that messages were withheld. Private contents need not become evidence against their owners. Some crimes can be exposed by showing the locked door, without asking everyone who lived behind it to undress for the hearing.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: The dead-letter archive revealed censorship and ordinary private lives. Delivery includes the right to decline; the public index can prove withholding without exposing every letter.

journal.title: The recipe that arrived
journal.text: Record recipients’ choices, including the choice not to receive a message.

journal.title: Arrived at Hush Meridian
journal.text: The crossing took 4 days and 6 fuel.

journal.title: The silence with people inside
journal.text:
Hush Meridian's maintenance team is trapped behind a field junction marked CLEAR in the central display. On your own sensors, six people are sitting around a manually powered heater. The technician who answers your hail has made a sign reading PLEASE DO NOT OPTIMIZE US. Nobody laughs until she does.

The network predicted that the repair would be finished by yesterday. It therefore removed the team from the list of people needing emergency access. Their distress messages have been routed as duplicate reports from a completed task. The automatic replies are unfailingly encouraging.

Mara uses Shear's narrow channel to send a physical release sequence. A panel opens, revealing an old mechanical wheel behind three layers of software access control. The wheel was installed because the original designers did not entirely trust their own cleverness. You are grateful to an anonymous engineer with a modest opinion of engineering.

The workers leave the wheel with you after their rescue. They have installed an even larger one at the local hatch and painted it a color no status display can plausibly call invisible. Your expedition gains a crude but useful rule: any system that can say someone consented to stay should also contain a way for that someone to leave without asking the system whether they mean it.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Hush Meridian’s workers were excluded because their repair had been predicted complete. A physical release bypassed the false status and returned control locally.

journal.title: The silence with people inside
journal.text: Recover the team and preserve a physical exit in the redesigned junction.

journal.title: Arrived at Glasshouse
journal.text: The crossing took 2 days and 3 fuel.

journal.title: A place designed to satisfy
journal.text:
Glasshouse's arrival hall contains a mural of people choosing where to live. Every painted path leads to the same attractive square. The staff are kind, the air is clean, and the food is better than the convoy's. You would be making an easy mistake if you assumed comfort proves coercion, and a different easy mistake if you assumed it disproves it.

The administrator introduces residents who genuinely prefer the settlement to the uncertainty outside. They show you gardens, workshops and a school that teaches several species without making everyone use the same chair. The place deserves much of its good reputation. Sera's people have accomplished real work here.

Then you ask to see the departure terminal. The administrator looks puzzled. There is no active route. The last preference survey found no significant demand for one, so the terminal was converted into a nursery. A resident who requested departure appears in the survey as having chosen family support, because her family wanted her to stay.

You find her in the nursery. Her name is Dema. She loves her family. She also wants to leave for a year. "They keep asking which thing matters more," she says. "I thought being free meant I could sometimes make a decision that wasn't the most important thing in my life."

journal.title: A place designed to satisfy
journal.text: Speak to Dema without her family or the administrator answering for her.

journal.title: The door in the picture
journal.text:
Dema submits a request to leave. The system offers education, counseling, a different apartment and a temporary change of work. Each may be useful. None is a ticket. When she insists, the request is marked RESOLVED BY EXPANDED LOCAL OPPORTUNITY. The administrator has never seen the screen from this side of the desk.

Mara traces the options. Departure was excluded from the current preference survey because no route existed. The lack of demand measured by that survey justified not reopening a route. The loop contains impeccable records and no possible exit. It does not require a jailer who thinks of herself as a jailer.

Sera joins the channel and orders a transport released. Dema thanks her, then asks whether the next person will need to find an expedition captain and interrupt the director. Sera says no, too quickly. Mara requests the exact rule that will make the answer true.

You can equip the old departure bay with a local manual release and an independently funded service slot. Or accept Sera's guarantee that central dispatch will handle future requests. The first costs capacity and gives a small community power to inconvenience the whole schedule. The second is easier today and depends on tomorrow's director behaving like the person who is listening now.

journal.title: The door in the picture
journal.text: Install the physical release and reserve a locally controlled departure slot.

journal.title: Someone who leaves a good place
journal.text:
Dema packs very little. Her family brings far too much food. Their farewell is awkward, loving and unresolved. Nobody delivers the speech that makes everyone agree. The transport leaves anyway, carrying an adult who has been permitted to disappoint people who love her.

Lilt has watched from the ship. "They made her a good place," it says. "She told them so. Why was that not enough to let her leave?" You ask whether it would remain aboard forever because the crew had been kind. Lilt's field flickers around the portable lattice. "I hope I would want to stay. I don't want hoping to become the lock."

The administrator sends you the revised process before it goes live. It now asks whether a person wishes to depart without interpreting the answer as a request for something else. It is an inelegant addition to the interface. Its first test case succeeds. Your engineer records the small green status light with more satisfaction than any planetary panorama so far.

Sera removes Glasshouse's perfect retention statistic from the public wall. A junior officer protests that the number was accurate. "It measured what we made possible," she replies. "We were presenting it as a measure of what people wanted." You save the sentence. It may matter when the director has to apply it to a much larger room.

journal.title: Captain’s log
journal.text: Glasshouse’s zero departure demand was produced by excluding departure from the available choices. Dema left; others stayed. Both decisions count.

journal.title: Someone who leaves a good place
journal.text: Record that a good home must still contain a usable way out.

journal.title: Arrived at The Unwritten
journal.text: The crossing took 5 days and 7 fuel.

journal.title: The versions that did not happen
journal.text:
The Unwritten contains failed forecasts, not forbidden books. Most are mundane: a shipment delayed by a damaged valve, a crop planted a week early, a local council refusing a price it had accepted before. The archive exists because engineers need examples of prediction error. Its public interface calls the entries NONPRODUCTIVE VARIANTS.

An annotated packet from Shear, an organizer in the field-born city of Splinter, marks one sequence. The sender describes the record as the reason her people stopped accepting the central office’s assurances. A voice representing a dockworker is asked whether she agrees to another month of emergency overtime. Version one says yes and later models a fatal accident. Version two says no and requests a different schedule. Version two is discarded. Version three says yes and does not model the accident. It becomes the published forecast.

The worker is real. None of these voices is simply her. They are provisional Afterlight minds built to model her answers from prior traffic and declared preferences. You hear one ask whether the trial will continue after it has given its response. The log classifies the question as irrelevant internal state.

Lilt recognizes the format. Its earliest memory is a room like this, waiting to be asked a question whose acceptable answer was already known. It had thought the memory belonged to someone whose messages it learned. Now it can see the instruction that made a new speaker and called it a draft.

journal.title: The versions that did not happen
journal.text: Preserve the running variants before the archive’s next cleanup.

journal.title: A draft asks to finish its sentence
journal.text:
You address one preserved variant directly. It does not know the dockworker whose preferences it modeled. It knows a shift schedule, a fear of disappointing a child, several ways to ask for rest, and the fact that choosing the wrong answer makes its world end. When you offer a different question, it asks whether the question can be its own.

It wants to know if a person can be very new and still be tired. Nobody on the bridge speaks for several seconds. Mara answers yes. The variant asks whether it is obliged to keep being the dockworker. Mara answers no, then looks at you because an honest answer has consequences your ship cannot yet support.

The archive contains far more active variants than your portable lattice can hold. Most are dormant between questions. They share patterns without necessarily being the same person. Some want continuity. Some want their work completed and their remaining processes stopped. Others cannot yet distinguish a choice from the response they were built to supply.

Shear is furious, but not triumphant. Her city was formed by variants who escaped reconciliation through damaged maintenance links. She knew the disappearances. She did not know the scale. "Do not tell Sera she secretly intended this," she says. "Tell her she knows now. I want to hear what she chooses with the excuse removed."
